source.title: Small-scale proxies for large-scale Transformer training instabilities
source.authors: Mitchell Wortsman; Peter J. Liu; Lechao Xiao; Katie Everett; A. Alemi; Ben Adlam; John D. Co-Reyes; Izzeddin Gur; Abhishek Kumar; Roman Novak; Jeffrey Pennington; Jascha Narain Sohl-Dickstein; Kelvin Xu; Jaehoon Lee; Justin Gilmer; S. Kornblith

record.tranche_reason: The study compares validation loss across Transformer architecture-scaling strategies, which bears on V4, but it does not test the original power-law scaling or compute-allocation measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper focuses on training instability, not scaling laws. Its architecture comparisons bear on V4. It does not fit or evaluate power laws for loss, test large-run loss extrapolation, or study compute-optimal allocations. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper is about training instability, not scaling laws. In one side experiment (Fig. 7, E.3) it compares final validation loss when parameters grow by depth only (d=512), by width only (6 layers) or jointly. That bears weakly on V4. Loss differences appear only in figures, with no numbers in the text. No power-law fits of loss are made, and no compute-allocation analysis is done.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that instabilities seen at large scale (attention logit growth, output logit divergence) can be reproduced and studied in small Transformers at high learning rates. Known mitigations (qk-layernorm, z-loss) work there too. Scaling trends of model characteristics can predict instabilities before they emerge. They make no claim about loss power laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study investigates learning-rate sensitivity and training instabilities rather than reproducing the original scaling-law method; its width/depth comparison uses validation loss and a learning-rate sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture-scaling strategy (joint scaling versus independently scaling width or depth) changes the reported loss comparison at the largest tested scale.

fits_no_version.finding: Max attention logit follows a quadratic trend with scale. Extrapolating it predicted that a 4.8B model would diverge at LR 1e-2, and it did.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling trends of model internals (activation and gradient norms) can predict instabilities at larger scale.

fits_no_version.finding: LR sensitivity rises with parameter count, and faster when scaling depth than when scaling width.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sensitivity of final loss to learning rate grows with model scale.

record.problems: The relevant architecture comparison is reported as figure-only here, and the text does not quantify the loss differences or state the exact parameter count for the largest compared scale.
record.rows_left_out: No additional directly relevant results left out.

untested.parts: Loss versus N curves are plotted (2.4e6–1.2e9) but no power law is fitted or assessed.
No extrapolation of loss to much larger runs is quantified. There is only a qualitative remark on extrapolation reliability in Fig. E.3.
There is no systematic fixed-parameter sweep of shape within a moderate range, and no quantified loss differences.
Other modalities and training regimes are not studied.
Fitting choices and the bending of curves are not studied.

missing.what: Fig. E.3 caption says joint scaling gives 'a more reliable scaling prediction when extrapolating' from models under 1e8 parameters. This is qualitative and figure-only.
Changing attention scaling from 1/sqrt(dh) to 1/dh lowers loss slightly at the smallest scale and raises it at the largest. This is a small architecture-detail effect.
Per-head versus model-dim qk-layernorm gives 'slightly better performance' for per-head.

record.verdict_notes: I gave no verdict labels: the only rows linked to V4 are cannot_determine, because the loss gaps are figure-only and the scaling paths use extreme aspect ratios. The reader's limits_scope label is unsupported. A qualitative loss ordering without magnitudes does not contradict V4's 'only slightly'. Row r2 should note that the text says depth-only beats width-only at the largest scale.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss trends in parameters, tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict losses of much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation trends.
The study compares width and depth scaling strategies, but does not systematically vary all architecture details at fixed parameter count across a wide range.
Downstream task performance or its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: Transformer models with joint width and depth scaling
rows.size_stated: largest scale tested; exact size not stated in the comparison text
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss under joint width-and-depth scaling with independently scaled width or depth, using a learning-rate sweep.

conditions.value: best loss in a sweep over learning rates

rows.baseline: figure-only comparison with independently scaled depth and width
rows.note: The text says joint scaling has lower loss than independently scaling depth or width at the largest tested scale, but the magnitude is only shown in the figure.
rows.check: The text says joint scaling gives the lowest loss at the largest tested scale, but gives no magnitude. So it cannot show whether the difference is 'slight' as V4 allows. This is a scaling-path comparison, not a controlled fixed-parameter shape sweep.

rows.subject: Transformer models with independently scaled depth
rows.size_stated: largest scale tested; exact size not stated in the comparison text
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss under depth scaling with joint width-and-depth scaling and width scaling, using a learning-rate sweep.

conditions.value: best loss in a sweep over learning rates

rows.baseline: figure-only comparison with joint width-and-depth scaling and width scaling
rows.note: The text states that joint scaling has lower loss than independently scaled depth at the largest tested scale; the loss difference is not quantified in text.
rows.check: Depth-only scaling (d=512, up to 96 layers) is an extreme aspect ratio, possibly outside V4's 'wide range'. The size of the loss gap is figure-only. The text says depth scaling beats width scaling at the largest scale (Fig. 7), which the row omits.

rows.size_stated: largest scale tested; exact size not stated in the comparison text

conditions.value: best loss in a sweep over learning rates

rows.baseline: figure-only comparison with joint width-and-depth scaling and depth scaling
rows.note: The text states that joint scaling has lower loss than independently scaled width at the largest tested scale; the loss difference is not quantified in text.
rows.check: Width-only scaling (6 layers, up to d=2048) is an extreme aspect ratio. The loss gap is figure-only and cannot be read.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
